job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Aaron Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, I read a chapter of my Bible and I'm at the office in Turlock by eight. It's a small accounting practice with four people, and I do bookkeeping and tax returns for farmers, a few dentists and the local feed store. The owner, Mr. Delgado, has known my family for 30 years, and I like that clients bring us pies at tax time. I live in a rented house with two guys from church, and I go to Lucia's family dinner every Sunday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about how you got the job and what you're saving for.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did accounting at a state university and got a good result. I did a short internship at a farm co-op in my last year. Mr. Delgado offered me a job through my father, who runs an auto repair shop in town. I'm saving to marry Lucia, who's a dental assistant, and I owe about 16 thousand in loans, but my parents can help me in a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a fad, like the paperless office that was supposed to arrive in the nineties. I'd tell the guys at church not to worry. Online I'd say nothing, because I don't use social media much, and I certainly don't use the AI chat things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think things carry on. People will still want a man they know to do their taxes. Mr. Delgado's clients like to shake his hand. The only thing that bothers me is saving for the wedding. A ring and a deposit is a lot on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work and be the guy who shows up early. I'd save 300 a month for the wedding and do a few extra tax returns on Saturdays in season. I'd study for the CPA exam over two years if the office helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Calm in the way you are when the ground feels steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save 300 a month. How realistic is that on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight but doable if I stay in the shared house and don't eat out much. My share of rent is 550. If the car broke down I'd need Dad's help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there any worries you'd carry even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wages. They go up slowly and groceries go up fast. Also, Lucia's mum is sick, and we may need to help with that.

say: I'd say it's a **fad**, like the paperless office promised in the nineties.
I'd tell the guys at church **not to worry**.
think: People still want a **man they know** to do their taxes.
The only worry is saving for the **wedding** on my pay.
do: Keep showing up early and doing **returns** for local clients.
Save **300 a month** and do Saturday returns in tax season.
Study for the **CPA exam** over two years if the office helps.
feel: **Calm**, in the way you are when the ground feels steady.
S0.quote: People will still want a man they know to do their taxes.
fieldNote: Aaron's calm is tied to **personal relationships** with clients and his boss.
His real pressure is the wedding budget and Lucia's mother's health.
He says he does not use AI at all, in line with his profile.

steps.text: Keep doing returns and bookkeeping for local farmers and dentists
Save 300 a month in a wedding account
Study for the CPA exam over two years
Plan the wedding with Lucia for the autumn after next

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd tell Mr. Delgado we should be careful about letting a machine near client files. I'd say we're a handshake business and should stay that way. At church I'd say I'm worried about what happens to young men starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the book-keeping and basic returns are the part that goes. That's about half my day. If the big firms and software do it for cheap, the farmers might switch, and Mr. Delgado would not need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder on the client side, going to farms, helping with their planning, being the person they call. I'd keep studying for the CPA, since a licence still needs a person. I'd also ask my dad if I could do the books at his shop and a few friends' small businesses for cash on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. It feels like I did everything right and the rules are changing under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're a handshake business. What happens if clients still want a handshake but pay less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the pay falls and so do I. Mr. Delgado would probably hold on to me out of loyalty, but I wouldn't want to be a charity. I'd rather prove I'm worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use the tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. If I did, I'd want to see them used for years by people I trust. I know that's slow, but my father always said never buy the first model.

say: I'd tell Mr. Delgado to be careful about machines near **client files**.
At church I'd say I'm worried for **young men** starting out.
think: **Bookkeeping** and basic returns, about half my day, are the part that goes.

Do **weekend books** for my dad's shop and friends' small businesses.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit angry, as if the rules changed after I did everything right.

fieldNote: Aaron's loyalty-based reasoning has a **limit**: he does not want to be a charity case.
He resists the tools on principle, using his father's rule never to buy the first model.
Weekend books for his dad's shop are a realistic side income.

steps.text: Visit client farms and help with their planning each month
Pass the CPA exam sections over the next two years
Do weekend books for my dad's auto shop and two friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing for a day and then ask Mr. Delgado what he plans. At church I'd ask for prayer, and the pastor would probably start a help fund. I'd tell Lucia that same night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the work I do is gone in two years. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. And I'd be angry at the big tech firms and the politicians who let it happen so quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending to rent, food and the loan payment, and push the wedding back a year if it had to. I'd ask my dad if I could work in his shop, since cars still need hands for a few years. I'd also ask Mr. Delgado for any weekend work he'd pass on, and I'd lean on the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep. It's the thing I've worked and prayed to avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the wedding back. How does Lucia take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd understand, because she's sensible. But her mother's sick and she'd been looking forward to it as something good. I'd hate being the one who delayed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does working in your dad's shop mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sweeping floors and changing oil with an accounting degree, and I'd feel I'd wasted four years. My dad would say it's honest work, and he's right.

say: I'd ask **Mr. Delgado** what he plans, then ask my church for prayer.
think: The work I do is **gone** in two years, and I won't pretend otherwise.
I'd be **angry** at the big tech firms and the politicians who let it go so fast.
do: Cut spending to **rent**, food and the loan payment.
Push the **wedding** back a year if it has to.
Ask my dad for work in his **shop** and lean on the church.
feel: **Alarmed**, unable to sleep, since it's what I've worked and prayed to avoid.
S2.quote: I'd be sweeping floors and changing oil with an accounting degree, and I'd feel I'd wasted four years.
fieldNote: Aaron's response is **family and faith first**: Lucia, his dad, the church.
His anger goes to tech firms and politicians, not to the machine.
Honest about the pride cost of shop work.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the loan payment
Push the wedding back a year and tell Lucia first
Ask the church and my parents for help with bills
Start work in my dad's auto repair shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough for people to get ready, and I'd start talking about it with Mr. Delgado. At church I'd say we should help our young people learn real skills, like trades and bookkeeping for small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. Five years is short for a man with plans. I'd be 27, hopefully married, with maybe a baby coming. That's the wrong time for the ground to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the CPA and try to get into advisory work, the part where a client sits across from you. I'd save 400 a month and put it in a savings account, not stocks. And I'd learn the hands-on side of my dad's shop on weekends, as a backup that nobody can automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can stand it. It gives me time to marry and still get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn your dad's shop as a backup. Is that serious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd learn brakes and oil changes properly. A job where I can fix a truck is one that lasts longer than a spreadsheet, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia about the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should marry as planned and be careful with money. I'd say a husband who has a plan B is worth more than one who hopes.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **get ready**, and I'd talk with Mr. Delgado.
I'd say church should teach young people **real skills**.
think: Five years is short for a man with **plans**, since I'd be 27 with maybe a baby coming.
It's the wrong time for the **ground** to move.

Save **400 a month** in a savings account, not stocks.
Learn **brakes** and oil changes in my dad's shop on weekends.
feel: **Anxious**, but I can stand it, because there's time to marry and prepare.
S3.quote: A job where I can fix a truck is one that lasts longer than a spreadsheet, at least for a while.
fieldNote: Aaron's **plan B** is hands-on work, which he takes seriously.
He fears the timing against marriage and a first child.
He prefers cash savings over investing, reflecting his traditional caution.

steps.text: Finish the CPA and move to client advisory work
Save 400 a month in a plain savings account
Marry Lucia as planned and keep a plan B ready

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the answer is to work hard and keep family close. At work I'd carry on. At church I'd say we should teach our children trades and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but not scared. By 2036 I'd be 32 with a wife, maybe two kids and a house, if things go well. I'd have to keep my skills useful, but ten years is a lifetime of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a CPA and build my own small practice, with clients who know me. I'd buy a modest house, save about 350 a month and keep a few years of cash. I'd also teach my own children to use their hands and their heads, and keep my church community strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I'd go about my life and keep an eye on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach your children to use their hands. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad taught me, and it's something you can always do. If everything changes, a person who can fix a pipe or a truck will not be the first one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you more worried in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If five years passed and nothing was ready, no plans, no training, no help. Then ten years would be a short seven, and I'd start scrambling.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time**, so work hard and keep family close.
At church I'd say we should teach children **trades** and trust.
think: I'd be uneasy but not scared, **32** with a wife and maybe two kids.
I'd keep my skills **useful**, but ten years is a lifetime of work.

feel: **Uneasy**, but steady, going about life while keeping an eye on the news.
S4.quote: If everything changes, a person who can fix a pipe or a truck will not be the first one out.
fieldNote: Aaron's long view is shaped by **family and faith**, not by tools.
He would teach his own children hands-on skills as insurance.

steps.text: Become a CPA and open my own small practice
Save 350 a month and keep a few years of cash
Teach my children to repair things with their hands
Keep dad's shop skills current as a backup job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because two years is too short for a young man to build a family on. What would help is firms and churches and families holding together, and honest work being available, like apprenticeships. I don't need a handout, I need a job that lets me support a wife.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I think this is natural. I don't, really. I think some people in big companies are pushing it for money, and the rest of us are told it's progress. I'd just like it to be slower and to be asked.

headlineQuote: I don't need a handout, I need a job that lets me support a wife.
portrait: Aaron, 22, is a **bookkeeper and tax preparer** at a four-person accounting practice in Turlock.
He shares a rented house, owes about **16 thousand** and is saving to marry Lucia.
Traditional and resistant, he never uses **AI tools** and trusts handshakes, church and family.
He moves from calm to **alarmed** at two years, with his dad's auto shop as the fallback.
He wants work, apprenticeships and community help rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years is too short to build a family on.
whatWouldHelp: Firms, churches and families holding together, and honest **work** such as apprenticeships.
